Parc des Celestins turns descent into a controlled visual spectacle. The Lego house adds public play to a utility shell. Michigan Theater preserves cultural fragments through an adaptive use that is also evidence of urban loss. Calgary’s parkade makes reversibility a structural requirement. “Architectural flourish” therefore ranges from surface identity to a plan for life after parking; those are not equally durable contributions.

The snout house puts storage in the family portrait

A snout house (L082) projects its garage toward the street so that the vehicle entrance dominates the facade. The front door may be recessed or turned sideways. The form often results from a narrow lot, a desire for a large attached garage, and development patterns that prioritise vehicle access.

The effect reaches beyond taste. A street lined with garage doors has fewer windows and porches facing public space. Driveways interrupt the sidewalk, reduce planting, and create repeated conflict points. Neighbours have fewer casual opportunities to see and speak to one another. A house can provide convenient, weather-protected access for residents while weakening the pedestrian life of the block.

Hiding every garage at the rear is not costless. Alleys use land and paving, detached structures can be less convenient, and rear access may be difficult on some sites. The comparison should therefore focus on the relationship between private storage and public edge. A smaller setback, side entry, narrower door, habitable room above, shared parking, or stronger front porch can change that relationship without pretending the car does not exist.

Flourish, invisibility, or transformation?

The curriculum asks whether more garages should be architectural masterpieces or as invisible as possible. There is a third option: design them for less parking and eventual change. A spectacular facade can make a harmful amount of car storage easier to accept. An invisible underground garage can preserve a good street while increasing project cost and encouraging driving. An adaptable structure can serve current demand without declaring it permanent.

Judge each case at three scales. At the object scale, is the building safe, clear, and well made? At the street scale, does it support walking and public life or present ramps and blank walls? At the city scale, does its capacity fit transport and land goals? Architecture matters at all three. Beauty cannot excuse a damaging system, but utility does not excuse ugliness, fear, or waste.

The transfer case is a proposed garage beside a railway station. More parking might let distant residents reach transit, but a large structure at the station entrance could consume land suited to homes and shops, feed traffic across walking routes, and make the first public view a vehicle ramp. A mixed plan might price long stays, protect accessible bays, add safe drop-off and bicycle storage, wrap active uses around the ground floor, and design level floors for later conversion. The solution comes from the full journey, not the garage alone.

Sources for this chapter: all six official architectural links: Temple Street (L076), Lego Parking House (L077), Parc des Celestins (L078), the Michigan Theater (L079), Garagenatelier (L080), and the adaptable 9th Avenue Parkade (L081); plus the official snout-house discussion (L082).

Chapter 5 - Finding the way through built decisions

Frank Lloyd Wright and Los Angeles’s Grand Park provide two different endings to the section. Wright tried to integrate the motor car into a complete architectural vision. Grand Park converted land shaped by parking and civic buildings into a public route and gathering place. Both cases treat the threshold between arrival and dwelling as something that can be redesigned.

Wright did not simply hide the car

Frank Lloyd Wright was fascinated by the mobility the automobile promised. The official article on cars living inside architecture (L083) shows how vehicles entered his houses, plans, and wider vision of decentralised life. A carport or integrated garage removed the detached shed and made arrival part of the composition. That could blur the boundary between vehicle, home, and landscape, but it also helped normalise a life organised around private driving.

The Frederick C. Robie House (L084), completed in Chicago in the early twentieth century, is a major Prairie-style work. Long horizontal lines, projecting roofs, bands of windows, terraces, and flowing interior spaces connect rooms visually while protecting privacy from the street. The plan does not erase every boundary. It layers them. Low ceilings can compress movement before a larger space opens; walls extend outward; furniture, windows, and masonry guide the eye.

Calling the house “natural” should therefore mean more than noticing earth colours or horizontal forms. It is a highly controlled composition on an urban site. Wright frames views and choreographs passage. The relationship with nature is designed, not untouched. A school inspired by the same principles might use sheltered outdoor rooms, connected learning spaces, daylight, and built-in furniture. It would also need contemporary accessibility, flexibility, safety, and community requirements that differ from a private 1910 house.

Grand Park makes the route itself public

Downtown Los Angeles’s civic centre sits across a slope between major government and cultural buildings. The official curriculum case on Grand Park (L085) describes how RIOS transformed parking areas and disconnected civic land into a linked public landscape. Terraces, stairs, accessible routes, fountains, lawns, planting, movable furniture, and strong colour create different ways to cross or remain.

The park’s nickname, “the park for everyone,” is an aspiration that must be tested through use. Does programming welcome different communities? Are shade, toilets, transit, and step-free routes available? Can people gather politically as well as recreationally? Who controls permits and security? Public space is not made inclusive once at opening. It is maintained through rules, budgets, events, and everyday tolerance.

The project also demonstrates conversion at a larger scale than the adaptable garage. Removing surface parking frees civic land for people, but visitors and workers still need ways to arrive. Transit, remaining garages, drop-off access, walking connections, and regional geography continue to matter. Reclamation works best as part of a transport system rather than as an isolated photograph of greenery replacing asphalt.

Grand Park also makes a useful comparison with Robie House. Wright’s layered thresholds guide a small number of residents and guests from street to private interior. The park must guide thousands of strangers across a public slope while allowing them to choose their own pace and purpose. Both use compression and release, framed views, shelter, and horizontal movement, but their accountability differs. A private house can reflect one client’s habits. A civic landscape must remain usable when a festival, protest, lunch break, family visit, or wheelchair route occupies it differently from the designer’s image.

How to propose a local conversion

Choose an underused lot only after observing it at different times. Record ownership, peak occupancy, surrounding destinations, shade, drainage, traffic, and community needs. A weekday-empty school lot may be full during events. A privately owned site cannot become a park through imagination alone. Temporary use can test demand: planters, seating, markets, play, or a “parklet” can reveal who comes and what conflicts appear before permanent construction.

Design the edges first. People must be able to reach the place without crossing an unsafe sea of traffic. Connect ramps and crossings, make entrances visible, provide shade and rest, and leave room for both programmed events and unplanned presence. Avoid hostile design that prevents lying down or gathering in the name of tidiness. If parking is removed, explain how essential access and deliveries will work.

The sidewalk as the first chapter of arrival

The section’s examples form a chain of decisions. The ancient raised path protects the pedestrian from the street. The moving walkway tries to mechanise the path. Abundant parking stretches destinations apart. Garages and snout houses give vehicle storage an architectural face. Wright integrates the car into the home. Grand Park reverses the direction by returning stored-car land to public movement and rest.

None of these forms is neutral. Each one teaches behaviour by making some actions easy and others difficult. A broad shaded sidewalk invites a walk; a blank garage wall discourages lingering; a free kerb space invites storage; a movable chair lets a group shape its own conversation. Infrastructure is a quiet curriculum that people study with their bodies every day.

That curriculum can be revised incrementally. A city does not need to wait for one heroic park project. It can repair a missing ramp, extend a crossing phase, convert one parking bay into seating, plant shade where heat blocks a school route, and measure who uses the change. Small interventions are prototypes of public priority. Their evidence can support a larger transformation, provided officials listen to users who are usually absent from traffic counts.

Sources for this chapter: the official links on Wright’s automotive architecture (L083), the Frank Lloyd Wright Trust’s Robie House history (L084), and RIOS’s transformed civic landscape as documented by Landezine (L085) and the studio’s Grand Park project page.

Final synthesis - The path is part of the destination

A city can claim that a school, park, shop, or station is open to everyone while the route quietly says otherwise. Missing pavement, short crossing times, garage entrances, heat, steps, and distance can turn formal access into practical exclusion. Conversely, a carefully designed threshold can support safety, independence, exchange, and delight before anyone reaches the front door.

The sidewalk is therefore not a minor topic beside the grand year theme. It is where “Are We There Yet?” becomes material. Parking policy changes how far apart places are. A moving walkway reveals that speed works only inside a suitable system. A beautiful garage shows that liminal infrastructure can carry memory and identity, while an adaptable one admits that today’s use may not deserve permanence. Grand Park shows that a route built for vehicles can become a place for people.

When an unfamiliar urban case appears in a round, follow the allocation. Which movement or storage use receives space? Which users can travel independently? What happens at the edges and crossings? Can the structure adapt when needs change? The strongest answer will not ask only where the sidewalk ends. It will explain the kind of public life that starts there.

regularGuides.title: Monkey See, Monkey Prototype
regularGuides.htmlContent:
Monkey See, Monkey Prototype

A prototype makes an idea visible before it deserves to be trusted. This guide follows the useful fakes, rapid models, generated apps, staged demonstrations, and hidden workers that complicate the route from “possible” to “ready.”

Reading the title as a warning about imitation

The title rewrites “monkey see, monkey do,” a proverb about copying an action without necessarily understanding it. Prototyping can look similar from the outside. A team imitates the shape of a future product, but the version may not contain the machinery, safety, reliability, or organisation that the real product will require. The imitation is valuable when everyone knows which question it is testing. It becomes deceptive when appearance is used as proof of a capability that does not exist.

This section therefore needs more than a simple sequence from rough to polished. A paper interface can teach designers more than a beautiful coded screen because users will criticise paper freely. A 3D-printed shell can reveal whether a handle fits the hand without proving that the final material will survive heat. A chatbot can generate a working demonstration in minutes while leaving security and maintenance problems for later. A person hidden behind an “automated” service can help test demand, yet also expose private information and create a false claim about labour.

The official links are not a bonus gallery. They supply the evidence needed to separate these cases. Students should inspect the early iPhone hardware, follow the prototyping cycle, understand Sarah Boone’s practical invention, read the warnings attached to vibe coding, see the operator behind the Mechanical Turk, and compare public demonstrations with later reporting about teleoperation. The recurring question is not “Is it fake?” It is “What is simulated, who knows, what is learned, and what decision will be made before real users carry the risk?”

Chapter 1 - From rough draft to real product

A prototype is an early representation built to answer a question about a possible product or service. That broad definition includes sketches, cardboard forms, clickable screens, coded experiments, and near-production units. The prototype’s quality is not measured by resemblance to the final object alone. It is measured by whether the representation is faithful enough to answer the current question without wasting effort on details that do not matter yet.

Start with the uncertainty, then choose the model

If a team is unsure whether people understand the order of screens in an app, a paper prototype may be enough. A tester points to a drawn button, and a researcher replaces the sheet to simulate the next screen. No code is required because the uncertain part is navigation. If the uncertainty concerns whether a hinge will bear weight, paper is the wrong medium. The team needs dimensions, materials, forces, and perhaps a physical proof of concept.

A sketch explores form quickly. Storyboarding shows a sequence of actions and the context around a product. A wireframe establishes information hierarchy without committing to visual finish. A mockup shows a more detailed appearance but may not work. A proof of concept demonstrates that a difficult mechanism is feasible, often without presenting a usable product. User testing observes people attempting representative tasks. Each term names a different answer to “What do we need to learn next?”

Low fidelity keeps the model cheap and easy to change. It can encourage honest criticism because nobody mistakes it for a finished decision. High fidelity becomes useful when timing, realistic content, detailed interaction, manufacturing fit, or emotional response matters. High fidelity too early creates attachment. Teams may protect polished work instead of revising the underlying idea.

The early object may look nothing like the product

The curriculum’s gallery of famous prototypes (L086) makes a strong visual point: an early test rig often exposes components, cables, controls, and supporting equipment that disappear from the consumer version. That difference is not evidence of failure. Engineers deliberately build access around the part under investigation.

The linked iPhone M68 prototype (L087) resembles a circuit-board workbench more than a pocket phone. A development board allowed engineers to connect displays, radios, controls, and debugging tools while keeping the new device’s industrial design secret. The visible bulk belonged to testing infrastructure, not the intended user experience. A scholar who judges it only by appearance misses its function.

This also explains why a prototype and a draft overlap without being identical. A written draft is an instance of the work itself: the sentences may survive into publication. A prototype can be a separate instrument used to learn about a future work. A foam model of a phone may contribute no material to the manufactured device, yet reveal where fingers reach. Both are provisional, but they preserve different kinds of evidence.

A cycle, not a straight staircase

The official prototyping cycle (L088) moves through concept, representation, testing, learning, and revision. Real projects may loop through those stages many times and use several prototypes at once. A team can test size with foam, software flow with a clickable screen, and manufacturing risk with a separate material sample.

Feedback is evidence only when the test matches the intended use. Asking friends whether they like a rendered image does not show that customers can assemble the product. Watching a tester complete a task while a designer explains every step hides usability problems. A good test defines the user, task, condition, and measure before the demonstration begins.

Failure is informative when it changes a decision. If the same prototype is repeatedly shown without modifying the design or test, the team may be performing iteration rather than learning. Document the assumption, observation, and next choice. This makes the unfinished route traceable.

MVP is not a synonym for careless launch

A minimum viable product is the smallest real offering that can test a significant business or user assumption. “Minimum” reduces unnecessary build. “Viable” means the version still provides enough value and safety for the people asked to use it. A minimum marketable feature is usually a smaller releasable unit that customers can understand and value. The terms are used inconsistently, so scholars should explain the function rather than recite a label.

An internal mockup may break without harming anyone. A public health service, payment system, or children’s product has a higher threshold because users can suffer from error. The ethical amount of completeness depends on exposure. Moving fast is not an excuse to transfer unknown risks to people who were told they were receiving a dependable product.

Transfer beyond gadgets

Schools can prototype a timetable on one year group, mark a proposed room layout with tape, or run a short version of an event before committing a full budget. Governments can use temporary street materials to test a crossing. Writers can table-read a scene. The principle is the same: make an assumption encounter reality while revision is still affordable.

The method fails when a pilot quietly becomes permanent without evaluation, when participants are not told they are testing something, or when a temporary result is generalised to a different population. Prototyping is not automatically humble. It becomes humble when the maker accepts that the model was built to be contradicted.

Sources for this chapter: all three official product links: the gallery of early gadget prototypes (L086), the iPhone M68 development hardware (L087), and the linked prototyping cycle (L088). The chapter uses them to distinguish a test instrument from a rough final product.

Chapter 2 - Fast models, real risks

Digital simulation, computer-aided design, and additive manufacturing have shortened the distance between an idea and a physical object. A student can alter a file in the morning and hold a new geometry in the afternoon. That speed changes who can prototype and how many alternatives can be explored. It does not eliminate engineering, manufacturing, or responsibility.

Rapid means faster feedback, not instant truth

The curriculum’s rapid prototyping overview (L090) describes methods for creating models directly from digital designs. A 3D printer builds an object layer by layer, which makes complex and customised forms possible without first making expensive production tooling. Designers can test fit, scale, assembly, and ergonomics before committing to a factory run.

A print is still a model of selected properties. A plastic part may match final geometry while behaving differently under load, sunlight, moisture, or heat. Layer orientation affects strength. Surface finish and manufacturing tolerances can differ from injection moulding or machining. If a team uses the prototype to answer a material question it cannot represent, speed produces false confidence.

Simulation has the same limit. A model predicts according to its equations, parameters, and input data. It is powerful when assumptions are validated and conditions are understood. It can miss unusual users, rare failures, or interactions the modeller did not include. Physical tests and real-world observation remain necessary when the consequences justify them.

A useful test plan separates properties explicitly. A printed inhaler shell can test grip and button reach without ever delivering medicine. A digital airflow model can compare internal geometry without proving that a patient will use the device correctly. A production-material sample can test chemical compatibility without answering whether instructions are understood. Only the combined evidence approaches readiness. “The prototype worked” is meaningless until the speaker names which property worked, for whom, and under what condition.

Sarah Boone started from an ordinary difficulty

The prompt pairs Thomas Edison with Sarah Boone (L089), an important correction to the habit of imagining invention only through famous laboratories. Boone, a dressmaker who was born into slavery and later became one of the early African American women to receive a United States patent, patented an improvement to the ironing board in 1892. Her narrow, curved, reversible board made it easier to iron sleeves and fitted garments.

The invention demonstrates problem fit. A flat table could press cloth, but it did not match the shape of the work. Boone’s design embodied knowledge from repeated practice. Prototyping is often strongest when the maker understands a specific user and task rather than beginning with a technology and searching for a need.

Her example also complicates stories of individual genius. Access to education, patents, capital, manufacturing, and markets affects whose model becomes a recognised product. Makerspaces can widen access to tools, but a printer alone does not supply free time, mentorship, safe materials, legal support, or a customer network.

What a responsible makerspace needs

A school makerspace should match access to risk rather than restrict creativity through vague fear. Hand tools, lasers, soldering stations, and 3D printers have different hazards. Training can be staged: an orientation, a demonstrated skill, supervised use, and independent permission for lower-risk tasks. Clear ventilation, material lists, guards, maintenance, emergency procedures, and adult supervision matter more than a sign that says “be careful.”

The curriculum packet adds the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration’s 3D-printing guidance, which discusses potential exposure to particles, gases, hot surfaces, moving components, and finishing chemicals. Risk depends on the process and material. Responsible access means understanding those differences, not treating every printer as either harmless or forbidden.

Digital files create other risks. A model may reproduce a patented part, a restricted object, or someone’s scanned body without consent. A design downloaded online may contain a structural weakness invisible in the preview. Tool access therefore needs an ethical conversation alongside physical safety.

Democratisation can still reproduce inequality

Rapid tools lower some barriers. A small team can test a shape without negotiating an overseas factory sample, and a student can learn by making. Yet commercial printers, reliable materials, maintenance, software, and expert time cost money. Well-resourced schools can iterate more often. Designers whose bodies and cultures already dominate reference data may continue to receive the best fit.

Inclusive prototyping deliberately recruits varied testers and pays attention to outliers. An adjustable handle should be tried by more than an average adult hand. An assistive device should be designed with disabled users rather than merely for them. An educational product should be tested under the connectivity and language conditions of its intended classrooms.

When to slow the cycle down

Early in exploration, many cheap failures are useful. As a product approaches real use, the test burden increases. Teams need traceable requirements, repeatable measurements, safety margins, and independent review. In regulated fields, validation asks whether the final product meets user needs while verification asks whether it meets specified design requirements. The exact vocabulary varies, but the direction is clear: confidence must become more demanding as exposure grows.

A good restriction is specific, proportionate, and teachable. “Only responsible people may use this” leaves authority vague. “Complete ventilation training, use approved materials, and obtain supervision for this machine” creates a path to access. The destination is not a locked workshop. It is a community capable of making without pretending that enthusiasm cancels consequence.

Rapid fabrication can also shorten the route to harmful objects, counterfeit replacement parts, or devices that look certified but are not. The answer is not to treat every file as dangerous. Makerspaces can classify high-risk categories, require provenance for safety-critical designs, prohibit claims that an untested part meets a standard, and teach users to document revisions. Responsibility becomes a design practice embedded in the workflow instead of a personality test applied at the door.

Sources for this chapter: the official inventor profile of Sarah Boone (L089) and the official rapid-prototyping introduction (L090), supplemented by OSHA’s 3D-printing safety guidance. These sources support access with defined safeguards rather than a general ban.

Chapter 3 - Vibe coding and the flood of new software

Vibe coding describes a style of software creation in which a person explains a desired program in natural language, accepts code produced by an AI system, runs it, and asks for revisions. The term became popular in 2025 and by 2026 covers everything from playful experiments to products built with AI assistance. That range matters. Using a model to explain one function is not the same as deploying an application whose maker cannot inspect any of it.

The interface hides the stack

The official IBM explanation of vibe coding (L091) describes how natural-language instructions can produce and refine software. The immediate gain is enormous. A beginner can make a working interface, automate a personal task, or test a product idea without first mastering syntax, package configuration, and deployment. Experienced programmers can offload routine scaffolding and explore alternatives quickly.

Yet a simple prompt may create a complicated dependency stack. The generated app can include libraries, authentication, database queries, cloud services, and code copied from patterns the user does not recognise. The interface looks small because the platform hides infrastructure. Someone still has to understand data flow, permissions, cost, licences, failure, and update paths.

Natural language is also ambiguous. “Make login secure” does not define password storage, rate limits, session expiry, recovery, multi-factor authentication, or threat assumptions. The model may produce a familiar pattern that appears to work in a demonstration while failing under attack. A prompt is not a specification merely because it is written in English.

Prototype speed can create production debt

For a disposable prototype, generated code can be entirely appropriate. It lets a team test whether users want the workflow before investing in robust architecture. The danger begins when the demonstration attracts real users and becomes the production system without a deliberate transition. Temporary shortcuts now store personal data and depend on packages nobody has reviewed.

Technical debt is not simply ugly code. It is future work created by an earlier decision. Some debt is rational when speed has clear value and the repayment plan is understood. Unknown debt is different. If the team cannot identify what was borrowed, it cannot estimate the cost of change.

The curriculum’s official concern about uncertain quality (L092) should be treated as a viewpoint, not a settled measurement of every generated program. The stronger claim is narrower: software that nobody understands is difficult to test, secure, maintain, and support. Quality depends on review practices, domain risk, user scale, and whether the builders can take responsibility after the first successful run.

Generated code also has provenance risk. A model may suggest a package that does not exist, an outdated method, or a dependency whose name resembles a malicious package. It may produce code that passes the happy-path demonstration while exposing an administrative function or sending data to the wrong service. Because the output is fluent, a novice may read confidence as verification. Every dependency should be resolved from its authoritative registry, pinned deliberately, scanned, and understood well enough that the team knows why it is present.

What testing has to cover

A generated application needs the same questions as hand-written software. Does it behave correctly for expected inputs? What happens at boundaries and under failure? Can one user access another user’s information? Are secrets stored safely? Do dependencies have known vulnerabilities or incompatible licences? Can the system be observed, backed up, restored, and updated? Is it accessible to keyboard and assistive-technology users?

Automated tests are useful only if they test the right behaviour. Asking the same model to generate the application and approve its own tests can reproduce one mistaken assumption twice. Human review, independent tools, user testing, and security analysis provide different forms of evidence. High-risk systems need stronger independence.

Maintenance begins before launch. Name an owner, document the architecture, record dependencies, and decide how reports will be handled. If the prototype has no path for support, limit its audience and lifetime. A link that works today is not automatically a service.

A practical validation ladder begins locally with synthetic data, then moves to a small invited test, a monitored beta, and wider release only after observed failures have owners. At each step, increase the realism of data and load while tightening logging, access control, backup, and incident response. The gate is evidence, not the number of prompts the maker has typed. A generated app that cannot explain its own data boundaries should not cross into a setting where those boundaries matter.

Should it be harder to get there?

Making software creation more accessible is generally valuable. People who understand a local problem can build a useful tool without waiting for a large vendor. Students can move from consuming software to questioning and shaping it. Disabled users can customise workflows that commercial products ignore.

The alternative to open access should not be a gate controlled only by professional status. Skilled programmers also create insecure systems. Better gates are attached to consequences: a personal offline toy needs little oversight; a public medical, financial, educational, or identity service needs review, privacy protection, and accountable operators. Distribution, not creation, is often the meaningful threshold.

A practical route from vibe to reliable software

Begin with a bounded problem and data that is non-sensitive or synthetic. Ask the system to explain the generated architecture and assumptions. Keep changes under version control so a working state can be recovered. Test one behaviour at a time, then invite a knowledgeable reviewer to challenge security and maintainability. Replace unexplained components before broad release. Document what the tool can and cannot do in language users can understand.

This route preserves the creative benefit of a fast prototype while refusing the fantasy that code becomes self-supporting when it appears on screen. Vibe coding changes who can begin the journey. It does not abolish the obligations attached to arrival.

Sources for this chapter: the official IBM overview (L091) and the curriculum’s linked critique of quality and maintenance risk (L092). The packet also points to security mitigations and an AI-assisted building platform; these are examples, not proof that all tools have the same risk.

Chapter 4 - The Mechanical Turk and the ethics of useful illusion

In 1770 Wolfgang von Kempelen presented a cabinet, chessboard, and turbaned mechanical figure that appeared able to play strong chess. The “Turk” toured for decades under different owners and defeated or impressed famous observers. A skilled human chess player was concealed inside the cabinet. The machine did not merely fail to explain its operation; its presentation actively redirected attention away from the operator.

A fake machine that asked a real question

The official history of the Mechanical Turk (L093) shows why the hoax matters to the history of artificial intelligence. Audiences already wanted to know whether reasoning could be mechanised. The performance made that future feel present, even though the impressive intelligence belonged to a hidden person.

The apparatus depended on more than a secret compartment. Its operator needed chess skill, a way to follow the board, controls for the figure’s arm, and procedures for remaining concealed while sections of the cabinet were opened. The deception was engineered. That is precisely why the case transfers well to modern demos: a convincing front end can redirect attention from the labour and infrastructure behind it.

Amazon later named its microtask platform Mechanical Turk, making the historical comparison explicit. Online requesters can distribute small tasks to human workers, often in ways that support data labelling and AI systems. The worker is no longer physically inside a cabinet, but human intelligence can still disappear behind a technical interface and low unit price.

The historical costume matters too. The turbaned figure turned an imagined “Oriental” other into spectacle for European audiences. The cabinet hid a person physically while the character helped audiences accept mystery as exotic machinery. Modern product language can perform a related erasure when it describes distributed workers as a neutral cloud or a tiny piece of “human-in-the-loop” infrastructure. A responsible account names who performs the work, where decisions occur, and what conditions make the apparent automation possible.

Wizard of Oz testing changes the ethical conditions

In Wizard of Oz testing (L094), users interact with what appears to be an automated system while a human secretly or partially produces the response. A voice assistant prototype may route requests to a researcher. A travel service may have staff manually assemble recommendations behind a polished interface. This allows a team to test usefulness and interaction before building expensive automation.

The method can be ethical in a bounded research setting. Participants can consent to a study without being told every hypothesis in advance, if withholding detail is necessary, risk is low, data is protected, and debriefing follows. The design team learns whether the service deserves further investment. The illusion is temporary and governed.

The same setup becomes troubling when customers pay for “AI,” share sensitive information under false assumptions, or depend on a service whose staffing cannot scale. Deception about capability changes expectations of privacy, speed, availability, and responsibility. A human operator may read material that the user thought was processed only by a machine.

Four questions for an ethical simulation

First, necessity: could the same learning be obtained without deception? A clearly labelled concierge prototype may answer the demand question. Second, exposure: what harm could occur if the simulated service makes a mistake or a person sees the data? Third, duration: is this a short test with a decision date, or an indefinite business model? Fourth, disclosure: who knows the truth now, and who will be told later?

Consent is not all or nothing. Researchers sometimes cannot reveal the exact hidden mechanism before a test because that knowledge would change behaviour. They can still state that the service is experimental, explain data handling, avoid high-stakes tasks, and debrief participants. Commercial customers deserve a higher level of clarity because the company is not merely observing them; it is making a claim in exchange for money or trust.

Debriefing should do real repair. It should identify the concealed mechanism, explain why concealment was necessary, let participants withdraw data when feasible, and provide a contact for questions or harm. If the team would be embarrassed to give that explanation, the test design is warning them before launch. Ethical review is not paperwork added after invention; it is another prototype test for the social system around the product.

What the prototype is actually proving

A human behind the interface can prove that users value the outcome and help designers learn the right conversational pattern. It does not prove that a machine can produce the outcome accurately, cheaply, or at scale. Those are separate technical and economic hypotheses. Teams make a category error when success of the human-supported prototype is advertised as success of automation.

The difference resembles a film set. A painted facade can prove that a camera angle creates the desired image without proving that the building would stand. Everyone on the production understands the purpose. The ethical problem arises when an investor, buyer, or user is invited to infer structural reality from the facade.

Trust is part of the product

A service can eventually achieve real automation and still carry damage from its earlier claim. Users may reasonably ask what else was hidden, whether their data reached unexpected people, and whether present capability is independently verified. “Fake it until you make it” treats arrival as erasing the route. Trust remembers the route.

This does not require banning every illusion. It requires naming the boundary between a prototype and a public promise. Useful illusion is a research technique with limits, records, protection, and an exit. A hoax makes belief itself the product.

For transfer, imagine a school testing an automated tutoring service with teachers secretly selecting responses. The arrangement can reveal which explanations students request and where a conversation stalls. It cannot establish that a model gives accurate independent advice, and it raises special privacy and power concerns because students may not freely refuse. Label the service as experimental, use invented or low-risk content, disclose human review, set a short test period, and compare the manual evidence with a separately validated technical system before claiming arrival.

Sources for this chapter: the official history of the Mechanical Turk (L093) and the service-design account of Wizard of Oz methods (L094). The chapter distinguishes a governed test from a commercial deception by purpose, risk, duration, and disclosure.

Chapter 5 - Demos, hidden labour, and the performance of readiness

A demonstration is a story about a product. The presenter chooses the conditions, sequence, camera, examples, and moment of success. That selection is unavoidable. A fair demo controls variables so a capability can be understood. A rigged demo controls them so viewers infer a capability the system does not have.

The dancer inside the robot announcement

At Tesla’s 2021 AI event, Elon Musk introduced the idea of a humanoid “Tesla Bot.” Before any robot appeared, a person in a white bodysuit danced on stage. The official curriculum links the costume reveal (L095). The absurdity was visible rather than secret, so it was not a Mechanical Turk style hoax. It was theatrical framing for a promised product. The risk was that spectacle and a confident timeline could make concept art feel closer to engineering reality than it was.

Later Optimus prototypes became physical machines, which is genuine progress. Public appearances still raised questions about autonomy and human assistance. The curriculum’s link on a robot “still not quite there” (L096) discusses teleoperation, while reporting around the 2024 We, Robot event found that human operators assisted interactions. Teleoperation is a legitimate robotics tool. It supports data collection, training, remote work, and safe testing. The misleading step would be allowing an audience to believe assisted behaviour was fully autonomous.

A good demo label can preserve both excitement and truth: locomotion is autonomous, dialogue is remotely assisted, the route is pre-mapped, or the task succeeds in a controlled environment. Those details do not ruin the achievement. They locate it.

Rigging has degrees

The official gallery of staged technology demos (L097) includes cases that should not all receive one verdict. A pre-recorded backup video used after a live failure is different from footage presented as live. A product tested on a carefully prepared route is different from a computer animation presented without disclosure. A human selecting from suggested responses is different from a robot generating them independently.

Evaluate materiality, not just the word “rigged.” Which component was real? What human assistance occurred? Were conditions representative of the claim? Did the presenter disclose the limitation before viewers made a decision? An engineering demo may appropriately isolate one subsystem. An investor presentation that implies the whole product works invites a broader inference and therefore owes broader evidence.

Amazon’s Just Walk Out case needs a correction, not a slogan

Reports about Amazon’s Just Walk Out checkout technology stated that about a thousand workers in India watched store video and helped determine purchases. The curriculum links the Ars Technica report (L098). That source is important because it made hidden human review visible, but scholars should also read the later Associated Press clarification.

Amazon disputed the claim that human reviewers were secretly acting as cashiers for every transaction. It said computer-vision models performed the checkout and human reviewers annotated video to improve the system and reviewed a minority of transactions. Human labelling and exception review are normal parts of many machine-learning systems. The serious questions remain: how large was the human role at each stage, what did customers understand about video processing, where and under what conditions was review work performed, and how did that role change over time?

Later evidence also prevents an outdated conclusion that the technology simply disappeared. In a September 2024 technical account, Amazon described a new multimodal receipt model and said Just Walk Out was operating in more than 180 third-party locations. That is Amazon's own dated account, so it should be read alongside independent reporting rather than treated as a neutral audit. It nevertheless shows why removal from many Amazon Fresh stores and continuation in other venues can both be true.

The accurate lesson is stronger than the viral one. “AI” often describes a sociotechnical system containing models, sensors, cloud infrastructure, remote reviewers, store staff, and support teams. The presence of people does not prove the AI is fake. Concealing material human dependence can still mislead customers and investors about cost, privacy, scale, and autonomy.

Fireflies and the human notes behind an AI promise

The curriculum’s founder account about Fireflies.ai (L099) describes an early service sold as AI meeting assistance while the founders manually joined or listened to meetings and produced notes. A later report highlights the privacy and deception concerns.

As a demand test, manual note production could reveal what summaries users value before expensive automation exists. As a paid service entering private meetings under an AI identity, it changes informed consent. Participants may speak differently if they know an unknown person can hear the conversation. Employers may have confidentiality duties. The founders’ later technical success does not retroactively give early participants the disclosure they lacked.

A disclosure ladder for prototypes and demos

At the lowest-risk level, an internal team uses a fake door or human operator with no external data. Basic documentation may be enough. In a recruited study, participants should know they are testing an experimental service, understand data handling, and receive a debrief if the mechanism was concealed. In a public beta, limitations, human review, and support expectations should be stated before use. In a commercial or high-stakes service, material dependence, privacy exposure, reliability, and responsibility require clear disclosure and stronger validation.

Companies sometimes fear that honesty will make a demo less impressive. That is precisely the test of trust. If a capability has value only when assistance is hidden, the audience is being asked to purchase an inference rather than evaluate an achievement.

How to watch a demonstration like a scholar

Write down the exact claim before the demo begins. Observe whether the environment is controlled, whether inputs were selected in advance, and whether a person may be intervening. Separate appearance, movement, decision-making, conversation, and endurance into different capabilities. Ask what happens outside the prepared route and how many trials failed before the successful clip.

Then look for dates. A 2021 concept, a 2024 assisted demonstration, and a 2026 product should not be collapsed into one permanent verdict. Progress may be real while the earlier presentation remains misleading. The year theme asks whether we have arrived; a dated evidence trail shows which “there” was claimed at each point.

Sources for this chapter: all five official demo and hidden-labour links: the 2021 Tesla Bot costume (L095), the later teleoperation concern (L096), the demo-history collection (L097), reporting on Just Walk Out (L098), and the Fireflies founder account (L099). The AP clarification qualifies the popular Amazon claim; Amazon's September 2024 technical account documents its later model and deployment claim from the company's own perspective.

Final synthesis - A prototype earns trust by revealing its boundary

The section begins with honest roughness. A sketch, paper screen, or exposed development board does not claim to be complete. Its unfinished form helps observers focus on the question being tested. As the guide moves toward public software and product demonstrations, roughness becomes easier to hide. A polished interface can conceal fragile code, a robot can conceal remote control, and an AI service can conceal human labour.

That does not make simulation the enemy. Wizard of Oz testing, teleoperation, manual concierge work, and controlled demos can reduce waste and teach teams what to build. Their legitimacy depends on scope and disclosure. The maker must know which hypothesis was tested. Participants must be protected. Viewers must not be encouraged to infer autonomy, safety, scale, or privacy that the evidence does not establish.

When a new case appears in an official round, ask four questions. What part is real? What part is represented or human-assisted? Who knows the difference? What evidence is still required before wider release? A prototype is not a promise that we are there. It is a disciplined way to discover what “there” would demand.

regularGuides.title: The Lovely and the Liminal
regularGuides.htmlContent:
The Lovely and the Liminal

A threshold can divide rooms, memories, identities, and stages of a life. This guide moves through the strange beauty of places that are designed for passage, then asks what happens when the passage becomes a world.

Reading “liminal” with enough precision to keep it useful

The Latin word limen means threshold. In social theory, liminality names a middle phase in which an earlier status has been left but a new one has not yet been secured. Online, the word often describes empty schools, fluorescent corridors, hotel carpets, foggy car parks, and other familiar places that feel detached from their normal use. Psychology adds another route: crossing a spatial boundary can change the information the mind keeps readily available.

Those meanings overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A railway station is architecturally transitional even when it is crowded and cheerful. A person awaiting a ceremony is socially between recognised identities even without standing in an uncanny room. A surreal painting can disturb ordinary categories without depicting a threshold at all. The section becomes interesting when scholars name the particular in-between condition instead of using “liminal” as a synonym for anything strange.

The official links are essential because liminality has to be experienced as well as defined. The Backrooms short film removes the expected destination from office-like corridors. POOLS makes a player move through echoing rooms without conventional goals. Paintings and photographs show railways as speed, crowd, atmosphere, and social theatre. Literature stretches a temporary wait into a condition of life. Ambient music changes attention without demanding the foreground. Read, watch, look, and listen before deciding what each work’s threshold actually is.

Chapter 1 - What in-between really means

The doorway effect begins with a joke nearly everyone understands: you enter a room and forget why you went there. The official prompt calls the doorway a liminal threshold and suggests that the mind “resets.” That is a useful image, but the linked experiment gives a more careful account. Memory is organised around events, and a boundary can signal that one event has ended and another has begun.

What the experiment compared

In the Scientific American explanation of the doorway effect (L100), participants moved objects in a virtual environment. Sometimes they crossed a room; sometimes they travelled the same distance through a doorway into another room. At selected moments they were asked which object they were carrying. Responses after crossing a doorway were slower and less accurate than responses after equivalent movement within one room.

The researchers also tested real rooms and found a similar pattern. Another condition returned participants to the original room after they had crossed two doorways. If forgetting came only from being in a different physical context, returning should have restored the advantage. It did not. The interpretation was that the boundary encouraged the mind to update an “event model,” reducing immediate access to information associated with the preceding event.

This is not proof that every doorway causes amnesia or that the brain empties short-term memory. Attention, task complexity, intention strength, familiarity, and individual differences matter. “Reset” is a metaphor for a change in accessibility, not a delete command. A scholar should preserve the experiment’s comparison: same distance, different event boundary.

Events need boundaries because attention is limited

The mind cannot keep every detail equally ready. It groups continuous experience into meaningful events: making breakfast, leaving home, travelling to school, beginning a class. Boundaries may be spatial, temporal, social, or goal-based. A door is a strong cue because new rooms often contain new actions and objects. Finishing a conversation, switching applications, or being interrupted can create a similar transition.

This explains why the effect is usually useful. Information from the old event becomes less urgent when a new setting demands attention. The comic failure occurs when one intention must survive the boundary but is treated as belonging to what came before. Carrying the object, repeating the intention, or writing a reminder can bridge the event.

Three meanings of liminality

Spatial liminality belongs to a route. A corridor, lift, bridge, airport, or waiting room connects places and is normally occupied temporarily. Social liminality belongs to a change of status. Anthropologist Arnold van Gennep described rites of passage through separation, transition, and incorporation; Victor Turner later developed the middle phase as a period in which ordinary roles may loosen. Psychological liminality is broader and less formal: a person between schools, homes, careers, relationships, or stages of recovery may feel that an old identity no longer fits while a new one remains uncertain.

Internet liminal aesthetics borrow from all three. Images often remove the people and purposes that make a place legible. A classroom at night is still a classroom, but without students, time cues, or a visible exit, it can feel like a memory of a category rather than an active place. The uncanniness comes from recognition without normal explanation.

Liminal does not mean empty

Anthropological liminality can be crowded, ceremonial, and highly structured. Participants may wear special clothing, follow instructions, and form an intense temporary bond because ordinary ranks have loosened. Turner used the term communitas for a form of direct fellowship that can emerge in such intervals. Whether it actually appears depends on the rite and its power relations; not every transition makes people equal.

This is an important correction to the online aesthetic. An empty corridor can suggest liminality, but emptiness is neither necessary nor sufficient. Frith’s crowded station later in this guide is transitional because many routes cross there. A graduation hall is liminal because a recognised status change is underway even when every seat is occupied. Analyse the process that suspends or changes roles, not the number of people in the image.

A threshold changes what “there” means

Before crossing, the destination belongs to the future. After crossing, the place may become ordinary so quickly that the previous intention fades. The year theme’s question can therefore be cognitive: how does the mind decide that one episode is over and another has begun? Arrival is not only a coordinate. It is an update in the model of what matters now.

That update can be chosen or imposed. A graduation ceremony marks a status change publicly. A refugee crossing a border may enter a legal and personal in-between that no ceremony resolves. A patient awaiting test results inhabits uncertain time. Calling all three “liminal” can reveal a pattern, but analysis must name differences in duration, power, and consequence.

How to test the word

When a new example appears, identify the before-state and after-state. Name the threshold or transition process. Ask which ordinary rules are suspended and whether the suspension is temporary. Then explain how the in-between changes memory, identity, behaviour, or feeling. If no credible before, after, or threshold can be identified, another word such as surreal, ambiguous, isolated, nostalgic, or uncanny may be better.

Precision does not remove beauty. It lets scholars compare why an empty airport and an initiation ritual can both feel suspended without pretending they are the same experience. Liminality is powerful because it describes structure: departure has happened, incorporation has not.

A small diagram in the mind helps: before, boundary, after. For the doorway experiment, the before-state is carrying an intention inside one event model, the boundary is the change of room, and the after-state is a newly updated context in which the intention is less accessible. For a social rite, the boundary can last days or months and include rules, teachers, ordeals, or waiting. When the middle grows indefinitely, it may no longer function as a passage at all. That failure becomes the subject of Chapter 4.

Sources for this chapter: the official doorway-effect account (L100), including its virtual, real-room, and return-to-context conditions. The social definition draws on the established separation-transition-incorporation framework; the guide treats “reset” as an explanatory metaphor, not literal deletion of memory.

Chapter 2 - Architecture built for passing through

Stations, trains, elevators, and waiting rooms are not blank containers around travel. They organise bodies, clocks, information, and expectations. Their architecture teaches people where to queue, when to move, whom to watch, and how long uncertainty should feel acceptable. The official works make that social machinery visible across more than 170 years.

Turner makes speed enter the landscape

In J. M. W. Turner’s Rain, Steam, and Speed - The Great Western Railway (1844, L104), a locomotive advances across Isambard Kingdom Brunel’s Maidenhead Railway Bridge. Rain, smoke, steam, and paint dissolve the boundary between machine and atmosphere. The bridge’s abrupt perspective pulls the viewer toward the train, making speed a visual force rather than a label.

The National Gallery notes a lightly painted hare on the track, now difficult to see because the paint has become more transparent. Natural and mechanical speed meet in one narrow route. The painting is not easily reduced to a rejection of industry. Turner used modern transport and treated the train and bridge as subjects worthy of ambitious painting. The liminality lies in a landscape being transformed by movement and in the viewer positioned between fascination and danger.

Frith turns the station into a social panorama

The curriculum names William Powell “Firth,” but the linked Royal Collection record correctly identifies William Powell Frith. His The Railway Station (1862, L105) crowds a large interior with travellers, workers, luggage, reunions, separations, and class signals. The station is not empty or anonymous. It is a stage on which private stories briefly share one public timetable.

Frith’s detailed groups reward narrative looking. Some people are leaving, some arriving, and some remain because working in the station is their destination. This challenges the simple claim that a liminal space belongs to nobody. A platform is temporary for the passenger and routine for the porter. Liminality depends on the user’s relation to the space.

Railways carry modernity into different visual cultures

Tsukioka Yoshitoshi’s Picture of the Railroad at Takanawa (1871, L106) depicts the railway just before Japan’s first line opened between Shimbashi and Yokohama in 1872. The woodblock print places new transport within a familiar print medium. Railway, shoreline, boats, and distant city make technological transition visible before the system has become ordinary.

Claude Monet’s The Gare St-Lazare (1877, L107) moves inside the terminal. Iron roof girders form dark geometry while steam turns an industrial interior into changing atmosphere. The National Gallery identifies it as one of twelve station views Monet painted that year. Light and cloud, conventions of outdoor landscape, appear under glass and iron. The station becomes both machine and weather.

The Yilan folk song “Drip, Drip, Drip” (L108), also known through romanisations such as “Diu Diu Tong,” connects rail travel with sound and local memory. Its onomatopoeic refrain is associated with droplets encountered as a train passes through a tunnel. Unlike the paintings, the route is carried in voice and rhythm. A tunnel briefly removes the wider landscape, and sound marks motion through the enclosed threshold.

A station can be theatre, image, and workplace

Steve McCurry’s Train Station, Agra, 1983 (L109) belongs to his extended journey on South Asian railways. The linked account describes the Agra Fort station at dusk, with the Jama Masjid mosque silhouetted beyond the train and an attendant adjusting a ventilator on a carriage. McCurry called the station a theatre where every kind of life appears.

The photograph’s threshold is layered. The carriage is about to move, the light is changing, the worker is performing maintenance, and the religious and transport architectures share the frame. Yet a scholar should also ask who photographs whom. A traveller’s image of a busy station can turn working lives into visual atmosphere. Liminal beauty does not cancel the unequal positions of observer and observed.

The elevator becomes an artwork while remaining an elevator

Richard Artschwager’s Six in Four (2015, L110) transforms four elevators in the Whitney Museum of American Art. The title refers to six recurring subjects in Artschwager’s work - door, window, table, basket, mirror, and rug - distributed through four immersive lift interiors. Visitors encounter the commission while moving to another gallery.

This is liminal art in a precise architectural sense. The museum does not ask everyone to stop in front of a separate object. Functional transit becomes the exhibition. The doors close, the view changes, and the artwork ends when the destination floor opens. Repeated visitors may experience different elements without scheduling a special encounter.

Waiting rooms design uncertainty

The official history of transitional “non-places” (L111) describes waiting rooms as political and social architectures. A doctor’s horseshoe of chairs directs strangers toward one another and the door. A government waiting area can sort people by legal category. Number screens, reception desks, closed doors, and rows of seats distribute information and authority.

The linked article on waiting-room anxiety (L112) focuses on colour, sound, seating, nature, and information. It is an accessible design discussion rather than strong clinical evidence, so use its claims as hypotheses. More robust principles can still be reasoned from the task: uncertainty feels worse when people do not know how long they will wait, whether they have been forgotten, or what will happen next. Clear check-in, progress information, privacy, comfortable seating, daylight, acoustic control, and visible staff can reduce some of that uncertainty.

Different purposes demand different rooms. An emergency department needs infection control, observation, triage, and room for distress. A child clinic may need play without overwhelming noise. A visa office needs clear document preparation and fair queue information. A bereavement setting needs privacy. “Calming” is not one universal colour palette; it is a relationship between design and the reason people are waiting.

Architecture sets the terms of temporary belonging

Across the works, movement becomes modern speed, social crowd, atmospheric uncertainty, national transition, labour, and art. The station is temporary for some and permanent work for others. The elevator is a few seconds of passage transformed into cultural encounter. The waiting room can make equal order visible or expose unequal bureaucracy.

When analysing a new transit space, ask how the architecture communicates time, direction, status, and control. Who can sit? Who can see the next step? Whose language appears on the sign? What happens when a delay becomes long? The beauty of a threshold is inseparable from whether people can move through it with dignity.

Four railway works, four models of historical time

Turner paints the train as an event bursting into the present. The viewer confronts a machine moving faster than familiar animal speed. Yoshitoshi’s print places new railway infrastructure inside a medium with its own established visual traditions, so technological change is seen through cultural continuity. Monet paints after the railway has become everyday enough to study repeatedly; modernity is now atmosphere, work, and changing light. McCurry photographs a mature network whose colonial construction history, national symbolism, maintenance labour, and ordinary passengers occupy the same station.

These differences prevent a single story in which railways simply represent progress. A line can connect cities and reorganise land, labour, time zones, class relations, military power, and access. The official artworks do not document all those effects by themselves, but they train scholars to ask which stage of arrival an image records: astonishing innovation, cultural transition, normalised infrastructure, or inherited system. The Yilan song adds memory from inside the journey, where the tunnel is known through echo and dripping sound rather than seen from an outside viewpoint.

Compare the frame, not only the subject

Turner’s diagonal bridge makes the viewer face the approaching engine. Monet’s station roof encloses steam and disperses attention among platforms. Frith offers enough detail to scan separate social stories. McCurry uses dusk and silhouette to suspend one working gesture. Artschwager removes the distant viewpoint entirely: the visitor’s body enters the commissioned lift and completes the movement. Every work depicts transit, but each assigns the viewer a different position - endangered observer, atmospheric witness, social reader, photographic traveller, or actual passenger.

This is a strong official-round method. Identify where the work places you, what information that position permits, and what it hides. A station map viewed from above creates mastery. A platform photograph creates partial waiting. An elevator installation gives no wide overview because its duration and enclosure are the work. Perspective is one of the tools by which liminality becomes felt.

A design audit for waiting

Visit or remember two waiting spaces and reconstruct the sequence. How does a person know they have checked in? Can they estimate the wait? Is the next name announced publicly, displayed visually, sent privately, or all three? Where can someone ask for help without losing a place? Are toilets, water, charging, interpretation, and quiet available? Does furniture assume one body size and one way of sitting?

Then separate anxiety caused by the future event from anxiety added by the room. A clinic cannot make a diagnosis unfrightening through paint colour, but it can avoid uncertainty about whether the patient was forgotten. A migration office cannot make a legal decision harmless through music, but it can give clear multilingual steps and protect private conversation. Good threshold design does not disguise power. It makes the process legible and reduces unnecessary suffering around it.

Sources for this chapter: every official shared-space link, from Turner’s Rain, Steam, and Speed (L104), Frith’s Railway Station (L105), Yoshitoshi’s Takanawa railway (L106), Monet’s Gare St-Lazare (L107), the Yilan folk song (L108), McCurry’s Agra station image (L109), and Artschwager’s Six in Four (L110), through the two waiting-room sources L111 and L112.

Chapter 3 - The uncanny ordinary

Liminal horror rarely begins with a castle or monster. It begins with a place that should be understandable: an office corridor, play area, hotel, basement, or swimming pool. The lights work and the carpet looks familiar, yet signs of purpose and human use are missing. The viewer recognises the category without being able to complete the situation.

The Backrooms remove the promise of the corridor

Kane Parsons, known online as Kane Pixels, released The Backrooms (Found Footage) in 2022 (L101). The short film presents fictional footage dated 1996. A camera operator falls into an apparently endless interior of yellow walls, fluorescent lighting, damp-looking carpet, and repeating turns. The corridor’s usual function is to connect rooms, but here each passage produces more passage.

The found-footage form narrows knowledge. The camera shakes, looks late, and records only what a frightened person could see. Visual noise and an old recording date make the image feel discovered rather than composed. Off-screen sound creates a threat before its source can be understood. The viewer shares the operator’s route and lack of map.

The horror is not emptiness by itself. An empty office during cleaning can feel calm because its time and purpose remain legible. The Backrooms remove ordinary explanations, reliable exits, and social witnesses. Familiar architecture continues after the story that once justified it has vanished. This is “not there yet” made terrifying because every step repeats the condition instead of reducing it.

POOLS creates pressure without a pursuer

The game POOLS (L102) describes itself through dreamlike rooms filled with pools. Its official site emphasises that there are no monsters, dialogue, conventional user interface, background music, or normal story notes. Water slows movement. Echo and sound change with the room. Architecture shifts as the player advances.

Removing a visible enemy makes perception the main activity. The player listens for a threat that the game says is absent, notices dark openings, and worries about being lost. Blue water, tiles, slides, stairways, and changing light recall leisure spaces, but nobody is playing or supervising. The environment has the form of hospitality without the social system that would make it safe.

Interactivity changes liminality. A film viewer can wait for the editor to reveal the route. A player must choose the next opening, accept slower movement in water, and take responsibility for entering a narrow space. The game turns uncertainty into an action without giving that action a conventional goal.

The Stanley Parable makes the route argue back

The Stanley Parable (L103) begins when an office worker finds that his colleagues have vanished. A narrator describes what Stanley does, but the player can obey or resist. Doors, corridors, lifts, and offices become arguments about choice. An ending may restart the game, and a choice may reveal that the narrator already anticipated rebellion.

The official site calls it an exploration of story, games, and choice, then undermines each category. That self-contradiction is the core mechanic. Stanley is between employee and player-character; the player is between author and subject; the office is between workplace and stage set. Arrival never settles authority because the game can reinterpret the route after each ending.

Unlike The Backrooms, this uncanniness is often comic. Both works remove colleagues from an office environment, but one threatens the body while the other destabilises authorship. A liminal setting does not dictate one emotion. The work’s rules, sound, camera, and relationship to choice determine whether uncertainty becomes fear, curiosity, humour, or critique.

Why abandoned and foggy places work so well

Architecture stores expectations. A school implies students, a pool implies swimmers, and a hotel implies staff and guests. Remove the people while keeping lights, furniture, and signs, and the mismatch demands an explanation. Fog shortens visibility, so the destination cannot organise present movement. Repetition weakens landmarks. Transitional spaces are especially effective because their meaning already depends on somewhere else.

Digital environments add impossible geometry. A corridor can loop without fitting inside a building. Doors can reload space. A narrator can remember a route the player reset. These violations are disturbing because they break the learned rules by which bodies predict safety.

Do not call every empty image liminal

An unoccupied room can be documentary, peaceful, neglected, or simply closed. A useful liminal reading identifies suspended purpose and unresolved movement. In The Backrooms, the endless route has no reliable destination. In POOLS, recreational forms remain while users and normal goals disappear. In The Stanley Parable, office circulation becomes a choice system whose endings refuse finality.

This standard keeps analysis from becoming a mood label. Describe the missing social script, the spatial rule that fails, and the effect on the viewer or player. The uncanny ordinary is not strange despite being familiar. It is strange because familiarity generates expectations that the work carefully denies.

Sound, repetition, and agency create three different traps

The Backrooms uses the camera’s incomplete hearing to imply pursuit outside the frame. POOLS gives environmental sound physical logic: echoes change with space and footsteps slow in water, so realism makes impossible architecture more convincing. The Stanley Parable replaces the hidden monster with an audible narrator who interprets the player’s action. In each work, sound tells the user whether the space recognises them, but the answer differs: something may be hunting, the room may be indifferent, or the story may be arguing back.

Repetition also performs different work. Yellow corridors erase landmarks, poolrooms vary just enough to make memory uncertain, and office routes repeat after endings while carrying knowledge from earlier play. The first weakens orientation, the second sustains exploratory attention, and the third turns repetition into commentary on choice. Scholars should name these mechanisms rather than concluding that all three games are effective because liminal spaces are “creepy.”

Agency completes the comparison. The found-footage operator appears to choose under panic, the POOLS player explores without a conventional objective, and Stanley’s player can disobey a narrator who may convert disobedience into another authored route. Increasing control does not guarantee arrival. Sometimes the work gives choice precisely so the limits of choice can be felt.

Sources for this chapter: the official Backrooms short film (L101), the developer’s POOLS site (L102), and the official Stanley Parable description (L103). Their shared architecture supports different emotional and narrative mechanisms.

Chapter 4 - Rites, thresholds, and unstable identities

Liminality is meant to be temporary. A traveller waits for a train, a candidate completes an initiation, and a guest eventually leaves the hotel. The works in this branch ask what happens when the expected incorporation never comes. Waiting can empty life, create solidarity, sharpen attention, produce humiliation, or become the condition in which a new self is made.

Waiting for Godot: repetition without arrival

Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot, including the curriculum’s Scene 2 (L120), keeps Vladimir and Estragon beside a road and tree while the expected Godot does not arrive. They talk, argue, remember imperfectly, consider leaving, and remain. The second act repeats much of the first with changes that make time both undeniable and difficult to measure.

The waiting is active theatre. Small routines prevent silence and give the pair reasons to continue. A messenger renews expectation, so disappointment does not become a final ending. The road promises movement, but the characters’ shared promise fixes them in place. This is a powerful model of delayed arrival because hope sustains the condition that hope is supposed to end.

Neruda’s stillness is a chosen interval

Pablo Neruda’s “Keeping Still” (L121) imagines a brief, shared pause in habitual activity. It is not an argument for permanent inactivity or death. The poem distinguishes stillness from total withdrawal and presents the interval as a chance to interrupt violence, labour, and misunderstanding long enough to perceive another possibility.

Placed beside Beckett, the poem shows that duration and agency matter. Vladimir and Estragon cannot convert waiting into arrival. Neruda’s collective pause is deliberately bounded and valuable because normal action will resume differently. Both suspend ordinary motion, but one is an unresolved dependency and the other a reflective practice.

A platform turns romantic hope into public exposure

Philippe Orreindy’s short film I’ll Wait for the Next One... (2002, L122) takes place in the Paris Metro. A man makes a public announcement that appears to seek love, and a woman decides whether to respond. The next train supplies a literal deadline. The platform is a place where strangers briefly share attention, then disperse.

The film uses that temporary public to make vulnerability visible. A private desire becomes a performance under the eyes of commuters. Waiting for the next train also becomes waiting for another chance, but transport time is indifferent to emotional readiness. The exact plot turn should be watched rather than spoiled by a guide; its value lies in how a scheduled departure converts hesitation into consequence.

Walking through walls does not abolish boundaries

Marcel Aymé’s “The Man Who Could Walk through Walls” (L123) follows Dutilleul, an ordinary Paris clerk who discovers he can pass through solid barriers. At first the gift barely changes his conventional life. Humiliation at work encourages him to use it, and freedom from walls expands into rebellion, crime, and a new public identity.

The story makes physical thresholds optional while social and psychological ones intensify. Dutilleul can cross a locked surface but cannot remain outside consequence. His ability eventually fails at the moment when passage matters most, leaving him trapped in the material boundary he once treated as meaningless. The fantasy proves that a threshold is more than an obstacle. It organises restraint, privacy, temptation, and identity.

The official page dates the story’s collection to 1943, rather than the 1941 date printed in the curriculum line. Scholars should remember the discrepancy instead of forcing false agreement. A publication date is a factual detail; the mechanism of the story remains the reversal from effortless passage to permanent entrapment.

The hotel becomes a whole world

In Amor Towles’s A Gentleman in Moscow excerpt (L124), Count Alexander Rostov is sentenced in 1922 to lifelong house arrest in Moscow’s Metropol Hotel. A hotel is normally a temporary home between journeys. The sentence turns it into the boundary of an entire life.

The opening movement makes the change architectural. Rostov is taken from his grand suite to a small attic room formerly used for servants. He must choose which possessions can fit. Status, space, and political order change together. The hotel remains open to travellers and historical change while he cannot cross its outer threshold.

Confinement does not freeze identity. Within the building, relationships, work, observation, and responsibility give time shape. This distinguishes the novel from a simple prison narrative. The passage-space becomes a community and vantage point. A person may not reach the expected destination yet still build a meaningful route inside the limit.

Temporary suspension can liberate or dominate

Rites of passage often loosen ordinary roles under recognised rules and then return participants to society with a new status. The five works remove or complicate that guarantee. Godot does not arrive. The shared pause is only an imagined possibility. A train leaves on schedule regardless of emotional outcome. A supernatural ability crosses walls until it cannot. A hotel stay becomes a sentence.

Power determines whether liminality is chosen. A retreat, gap year, or quiet interval can support reflection because the person has resources and an exit. Detention, bureaucratic delay, displacement, and indefinite waiting impose uncertainty. Describing both as liminal should not flatten the difference between seeking an interval and being denied incorporation.
